hook.line: Don Hernando's oldest friend is leaving Bogotá, and he can't quite say goodbye. This is the soft way to tell someone that their news makes you sad.
hook.es: Me da mucha pena que te vayas tan pronto.
hook.en: It makes me so sad that you're leaving so soon. (to a friend)

examples.es: Me da pena que estés solo.
examples.en: It makes me sad that you're alone. (to a friend)
What a shame you can't come! (to a friend)

examples.es: Me da mucha pena que Rosa no esté aquí.
examples.en: It makes me very sad that Rosa isn't here.
What a shame they're closing the café!

examples.es: Nos da pena que no vengas.
examples.en: It makes us sad that you're not coming. (to a friend)

examples.es: Me da pena hablar delante de todos.
examples.en: I'm embarrassed to speak in front of everyone.

rule:
*Me da pena que* plus the wish form says what someone else's news makes you feel: *Me da pena que estés solo.* Swap *pena* for *lástima* and it means the same.

For a quick reaction, start with *¡Qué pena que…!* or *¡Qué lástima que…!*

In Colombia *pena* also means embarrassment, especially with an infinitive: *Me da pena hablar delante de todos.* *Lástima* is always sadness, so use it when you want no confusion.
smallPrint: Same "backwards" grammar as *gustar*: the sadness is what's given to you, so *me, te, le, nos, les* say who feels it.

options: It makes me sad that you're alone. (to a friend)
I'm embarrassed to be alone.

I'm embarrassed to speak in front of everyone.

options: It makes me sad that you're not coming. (to a friend)
It makes us sad that she's not coming.

options: It's such a shame I'm leaving.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *estás* or *estés* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Me da pena que ___ solo.*
yourTurn.answer: Me da pena que estés solo.
yourTurn.why: After *me da pena que*, the verb takes the wish form: *estés*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: What a shame you can't come!
yourTurn.why: *Qué pena que* plus the wish form of *poder*: *puedas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it with *lástima* instead: *Me da pena que Rosa no esté aquí.*
yourTurn.answer: Me da lástima que Rosa no esté aquí.
yourTurn.why: *Lástima* swaps in for *pena* and nothing else changes.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm embarrassed to speak in front of everyone.
yourTurn.answer: Me da pena hablar delante de todos.
yourTurn.why: It's your own action, so no *que*: just the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about don Hernando: *Me da pena que Rosa no esté.*
yourTurn.answer: A don Hernando le da pena que Rosa no esté.
yourTurn.why: *Me* becomes *le*, and *A don Hernando* says who feels it.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It makes us sad that you're not coming. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: Nos da pena que no vengas.
accept: Nos da lástima que no vengas.
yourTurn.why: For *we*, *me* becomes *nos*, and *vengas* is the wish form for *tú*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *cierran* or *cierren* and type the whole sentence: *¡Qué lástima que ___ el café!*
yourTurn.why: *Qué lástima que* wants the wish form, so *cierren*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me da pena que estás solo.
pitfalls.right: Me da pena que estés solo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After a feeling about someone else, use the wish form: *estés*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo pena que no puedas venir.
pitfalls.right: Me da pena que no puedas venir.
pitfalls.why: Spanish doesn't "have" the sadness. It's given to you: *me da pena*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me da pena que hablar delante de todos.
pitfalls.right: Me da pena hablar delante de todos.
pitfalls.why: Almost. When you're the one acting, drop *que* and use the infinitive.

personal: Tell us something that makes you a little sad about someone else's situation. For example: *Me da pena que mis amigos vivan lejos.*
